Why Are Two MOSFETs Connected Back-to-Back in a MOSFET Circuit? by: Mila Nov 12,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout mosfet circuit MOSFET Body Diode Back-to-Back MOSFETs Bidirectional MOSFET Switch Reverse Current Blocking In PCB design , MOSFETs are widely used in power management circuits to control current flow, protect power sources, and manage power switching. However, when a circuit needs to support both charging and discharging while preventing unwanted reverse current, a single MOSFET may not be sufficient. This is where two back-to-back MOSFETs come into play. By connecting two MOSFETs in series with oppositely oriented body diodes, designers can create a bidirectional switch that allows current to flow in both directions when turned on and blocks current in either direction when turned off. This article explains how this configuration works and why it is useful in PCB power circuit design. 1. What Is a Bidirectional Switch? A bidirectional switch is a switching circuit built using MOSFETs, IGBTs, or other power semiconductor devices. It allows current to flow in either direction when turned on and blocks current in both directions when turned off. For example, when point A has a positive voltage and point B has a negative voltage, current can flow from A to B. When the voltage polarity reverses, with A becoming negative and B positive, the current direction also reverses, allowing current to flow from B to A. A bidirectional switch can be constructed by connecting two MOSFETs or IGBTs back-to-back. （Back-to-back MOSFET circuit） So, how does this configuration allow current to flow in both directions? 2. How Do Back-to-Back MOSFETs Enable Bidirectional Conduction? Let's use a circuit that supports both USB-to-battery charging and battery-to-USB power delivery as an example. Charging the Battery from USB When the USB power source charges the battery, the USB-side voltage is higher than the battery-side voltage. In this condition, Q3 turns on, and the USB power source establishes an initial current path through the body diode of Q1 and Q3. The control circuit then applies sufficient gate drive voltage to Q1 and Q2, turning both MOSFETs on. Once both MOSFETs are on, current flows through their conducting channels to the battery, allowing it to charge. Powering a USB Load from the Battery When the battery supplies power to an external USB load, the current flows in the opposite direction. Q3 turns on, allowing an initial current path to form through the body diode of Q2 and Q3. The control circuit then drives Q1 and Q2 on, allowing current to flow through both MOSFET channels toward the USB interface and power the external load. Blocking Reverse Current When Turned Off When Q3 is turned off, the charging and discharging paths are interrupted. The USB power source can no longer charge the battery, and the battery can no longer supply power to the external USB load. This provides reverse current blocking, also known as reverse current protection, preventing unwanted current from flowing back into the power source. It is important to note that the body diode does not automatically turn on the MOSFET channel. Actual MOSFET conduction depends on the gate-to-source voltage (VGS) and the control circuit's operating logic. （The Principle of Reverse Current Blocking） 3. Why Use Two Back-to-Back MOSFETs Instead of One? To understand this, we first need to look at an important MOSFET characteristic: the body diode. A MOSFET has an intrinsic body diode. In a typical N-channel enhancement-mode MOSFET, the body diode's anode is connected to the source (S), and its cathode is connected to the drain (D). This means that even when the MOSFET is turned off, its body diode can still conduct current under the right voltage conditions. Using a Single MOSFET When only one MOSFET is used, turning it off closes its conducting channel, but the body diode remains present. For example, suppose the battery is connected to the source side of the MOSFET and the external load is connected to the drain side. If the source voltage becomes higher than the drain voltage by enough to forward-bias the body diode, the diode conducts. Current can still flow from the battery to the external load through the body diode, so the MOSFET cannot fully block current in this direction. Therefore, a single MOSFET can conduct current in both directions when turned on, but it cannot block current in both directions when turned off. Using Two Back-to-Back MOSFETs When two MOSFETs are connected back-to-back, their body diodes face opposite directions. When both MOSFETs are turned on, their conducting channels are enabled, allowing current to flow from either side to the other. This provides bidirectional conduction. When both MOSFETs are turned off, the oppositely oriented body diodes provide bidirectional blocking. Regardless of which side has the higher voltage, one of the body diodes will be reverse-biased, preventing current from flowing through the series path. Therefore, two back-to-back MOSFETs can provide both bidirectional conduction and bidirectional blocking. Single MOSFET vs. Back-to-Back MOSFETs The main differences between these two configurations can be summarized as follows: （Single MOSFET vs. Back-to-Back MOSFETs） Conclusion Back-to-back MOSFETs provide an effective way to achieve bidirectional switching and reverse current blocking in power management circuits. Unlike a single MOSFET, this configuration can block current in either direction when turned off while allowing bidirectional conduction when both MOSFETs are on. For PCB design , understanding MOSFET body diode orientation and the operating states of each MOSFET is essential when designing battery charging and discharging circuits, power-path management systems, and other applications that require reliable current control.
